questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether federal grants may fund state-owned property
questions.stem: Card 4 - our group debated whether federal grant money may pay for a new building that the state would own and operate. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Yes - federal money may fund state-owned property, since the state buys and runs it for its own purposes.
No - federal money may never buy property, because ownership must stay with the federal government.
options.misconception: assumes federal grants cannot fund state assets

options.text: No - a state may not use grant funds on buildings unless it gives up ownership.
options.misconception: invents a federal ownership requirement

options.text: Only if the federal government chooses the site and approves every design detail.
options.misconception: adds a federal approval step for spending

questions.explanation: Federal grants may fund property the state owns and uses for its own purposes, which is spending rather than commandeering. The federal government need not own the asset or approve its design.
questions.hint: Ask who owns and uses the building.

State employers are free from all federal employment law, as the dismissals suggest.
options.misconception: generalizes from mixed outcomes

options.text: The sample shows that state employees can never obtain relief in federal court.
options.misconception: ignores the settled and merits cases

questions.explanation: Federal employment law applies to state employers as employers, and one case reached the merits on that footing. The sample shows a limit on damages, not on federal reach in general.

questions.topic: State share of a matching grant
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a state satisfies the state share of a matching grant
questions.stem: Whiteboard note 3 - we asked how the state's share works when the federal government matches state spending on clinics.

answer.exemplar: A matching grant reimburses the state for a stated share of the costs it has already spent, so the federal share is calculated from allowable costs at the statutory rate and the state bears the remainder. The state must actually spend and document its share, because matching funds reimburse documented expenditure rather than replacing state effort with federal money.

questions.explanation: Federal matching funds reimburse documented state expenditure at the statutory rate, and the state provides the balance. Reimbursement follows spending, so unspent money cannot be matched.
questions.hint: Ask what the match reimburses.

Receipts exceeded spending by 7,500,000 dollars, leaving a surplus for the year.

questions.stem: Flashcard 21 - we wrote that federal grants usually come with an anti-supplanting clause. What does that clause do?

options.text: It caps how much of a state budget may come from federal grants.
options.misconception: turns an anti-supplanting clause into a spending cap

options.text: It bars federal money from replacing state funds that the state would otherwise spend.
It requires the state to return federal money whenever its own revenue rises.
options.misconception: invents a clawback tied to state revenue

options.text: It lets the state reduce its own spending if federal grants increase by the same amount.
options.misconception: allows dollar-for-dollar substitution

questions.explanation: Anti-supplanting clauses keep federal money from replacing state spending that would otherwise occur, so the grant supplements state effort. They neither cap the federal share nor allow dollar-for-dollar substitution.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit on withholding appropriated funds
questions.stem: Review board 15 - we asked whether the executive branch may delay or refuse to spend money that Congress appropriated.

answer.exemplar: Congress has the power of the purse, so funds it has appropriated cannot be withheld by the executive branch, and a refusal to spend is a constitutional violation rather than a permissible budget tool. The executive may withhold a limited amount for a short period while awaiting a signature, but it may not withhold funds permanently or indefinitely without Congress acting.

questions.explanation: Appropriated money is available to spend, so the executive branch may not hold it back as a bargaining device. A brief delay awaiting a signature is allowed, but a lasting refusal to spend is not.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the power of the purse.

questions.stem: Practice set 18 - we read the summary of the automatic reduction provision. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Any automatic reduction is unlawful, because Congress may not alter grants after they are made.
options.misconception: treats formula adjustments as retroactive changes

options.text: Automatic reductions tied to a funding formula do not require the federal government to command state officers.
Automatic reductions are lawful only if the state was warned and given a chance to fix the problem.
options.misconception: assumes a hearing is always required by the program

options.misconception: requires a formal finding for a formula-driven cut

questions.explanation: Congress may set the terms on which money flows, including automatic formula-driven reductions, because the state participates on those terms. The provision does not command state officers to administer a program.

questions.stem: Card 31 - we asked whether the executive may treat an appropriation as if it were a request rather than a command.

answer.exemplar: An appropriation is a command to spend, not a request, because the legislature has decided the amount and the executive's task is to carry it out. Allowing the executive to withhold funds would let the executive rewrite the budget, which is a decision the constitution assigns to the legislature, and would make the level of federal spending depend on negotiation rather than on law.

questions.explanation: An appropriation is a decision to spend that the executive must carry out, so withholding it would move budget control into the executive branch. Spending levels follow the law, not negotiation.
questions.hint: Ask whether an appropriation permits discretion.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A confound in a grant comparison
questions.learningObjective: Adjust a grant comparison for a population confound
questions.stem: Handout 50 - two states shared a pot of 9,000,000 dollars for a programme, and state A had 90,000 eligible residents while state B had 210,000. If the money were divided in proportion to residents, how many dollars per resident would each state receive?
questions.explanation: The combined eligible population is 300,000, and dividing the 9,000,000 pot by that total gives 30 dollars per resident. A proportional division gives every resident the same amount.
questions.hint: Add the residents, then divide the pot.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyze the legality of automatic formula-driven grant reductions

stimulus.body: Program summary: each state's award is fixed by a statutory formula, and a state that fails a federal standard has its award cut automatically by a stated percentage for the next funding period, with the cut ending once the state's reporting shows the standard is met. The summary states that the determination relies on data the states submit under the program, and that no federal officer carries out any part of the standard.

questions.stem: Practice set 70 - we finished the revision round on this clause. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The cut is invalid, because the state never agreed to a cut it did not negotiate.
options.misconception: treats a formula term as needing negotiation

options.text: The cut is valid only if a federal agency makes the determination by hand.
options.misconception: requires an adjudication for a formula cut

options.text: The cut is invalid, because no notice is given before it takes effect.
options.misconception: assumes a notice requirement the summary omits

options.text: The cut is a formula term built on state-reported data, and it commands no state officer to act.

questions.explanation: The cut is a formula term that operates on data the state itself submits, so it neither needs adjudication nor orders state officers to act. A state that does not want the cut can simply meet the standard.
questions.hint: Ask whose data drives the cut.
